analysis.one_liner: Bars the largest online platforms from buying current or potential competitors.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill in June 2021, but it never received a vote on the House floor and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unlawful for the very largest online platforms — those with at least 50 million U.S. users and over $600 billion in sales or market value that businesses depend on to reach customers — to buy other companies outright, unless the platform can prove the deal does not hurt competition. Today, dominant platforms can buy promising rivals, including small startups that might one day challenge them. The bill would flip the burden of proof: the platform, not the government, would have to show an acquisition is harmless, and regulators, state attorneys general, and private parties could sue to block deals and recover triple damages.
analysis.who_benefits: Small businesses and app developers that rely on big platforms to reach customers, startups that build products in markets dominated by a big platform (they keep the option to grow or be acquired by someone other than the dominant firm), and consumers who benefit when competitors can survive rather than being bought up. Antitrust enforcers at the FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general gain a clearer rule to act on.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small businesses, startups, and app developers

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for a covered platform — one with at least 50 million U.S. monthly users (or 100,000 business users), owned by a company over $600 billion in sales or market cap, that is a critical trading partner for businesses on the platform — to buy the stock or assets of another company.

Shifts the burden of proof: the platform must demonstrate by clear and convincing evidence that the acquisition does not compete with it, does not constitute nascent or potential competition, and does not enhance its market position — and competition for a user's attention and access to additional data count as competition for this purpose.

Gives the FTC and Justice Department enforcement powers, lets state attorneys general sue on behalf of residents, and allows any injured person to recover triple damages plus attorney's fees, with the D.C. Circuit handling appeals of designations and orders.

analysis.who_pays: The dominant platforms themselves, whose acquisition-driven growth strategy would be curtailed: large tech firms regularly buy smaller companies to add features, enter new markets, and eliminate potential rivals. Startups would lose one common exit route — being bought by a tech giant — and venture investors who fund them would face that reduced exit option. Consumers could also face a cost if the ban blocks some acquisitions that would have produced genuine efficiencies or new features.
analysis.who_pays_short: Dominant tech platforms and venture-backed startups

drawbacks.text: The ban is close to absolute: a platform can escape it only by proving by clear and convincing evidence that a deal fails every one of several competition tests, so even acquisitions unrelated to the platform's market position carry heavy legal risk, and the platform's access to extra data alone can count against it.

A flat ban on acquisitions rather than a case-by-case test could block some deals that benefit users or new entrants, and would remove a common exit for venture-backed startups, which investors in the tech ecosystem argue dampens funding for new products built around these platforms.

The designation system leaves a platform 'covered' for 10 years unless regulators remove the label, and channels all appeals through the D.C. Circuit with agency fact-findings treated as conclusive if supported by evidence — concentrated power in both the agencies and one court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea addresses a real problem: dominant platforms buying nascent rivals has been a recurring competition concern, and shifting the burden of proof matches the practical difficulty regulators face in proving harm from deals that haven't taken effect yet. The honest cost is that the remedy is blunt — a near-per-se ban with a heavy escape burden can sweep in deals that wouldn't have hurt competition, and it narrows exit options for startups. On balance the design targets a specific, concentrated harm (the handful of firms over $600 billion), and the main objection is about overreach in edge cases, not the direction of the bill.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee held markups and voted the bill out for a floor report in June 2021, but House leadership never brought it to the floor, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced June 11, 2021 by Rep. Hakeem Jeffries with Reps. Buck, Cicilline, Nadler, and Gooden as original cosponsors, and referred to the House Judiciary Committee.
The committee held markup sessions on June 23 and 24, 2021, and on June 24 ordered the bill to be reported to the House in amended form.
No further action followed: the bill was never reported to the full House, never scheduled for a floor vote, and received no action in the Senate before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
It carried 24 cosponsors — 19 Democrats and 5 Republicans — giving it bipartisan sponsorship even as it stalled in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The dominant tech platforms, which keep their ability to acquire rivals without the new burden of proof, and the status quo for their acquisition strategy. Nothing changed for small businesses or startups facing the same market conditions the bill targeted.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: the bill was introduced by a Democrat alongside two Republicans, and 5 of its 24 cosponsors were Republicans [S3][S4]; the opposition that mattered came from House leadership scheduling and outside tech lobbying rather than a party-line vote, since no vote ever occurred.

industries.industry: Dominant tech platforms (Google, Amazon, Apple, Meta)
industries.note: These are the companies the $600 billion threshold and 'critical trading partner' test were built to capture; the bill would end their ability to buy rivals and startups outright. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against the small businesses and app developers who must use their platforms to reach customers.

industries.industry: Small businesses and app developers on large platforms
industries.note: Businesses that depend on dominant platforms to reach customers — the bill's 'business users' — gain a shield against platforms using acquisitions to tighten their grip on the marketplaces those businesses rely on.

Startups competing with dominant platforms would keep room to grow instead of being bought, but the ban also removes the tech giants as the most common acquirer — reducing a standard exit for founders and their investors. The bill targets precisely the deals where this trade-off bites hardest.
